en: The Sūtra on King Virūḍhaka Spoken by the Buddha, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Yuezhi during the Western Jin Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Śākya Monastery in Kapilavastu. Ni...
Beneath the Kakudha tree, he was accompanied by five hundred bhikṣus, his attendant Ānanda, and the Vajrapāṇi Lohitya.
Within the city, there were five hundred elders from the noble Śākya clan who had collectively built a lecture hall for the World-Honored One. They made a mutual vow:

"Once this hall is completed, we shall invite the Perfectly Enlightened One to receive offerings therein. No śramaṇas, brahmins, elders, householders, or common people shall ascend this hall before the Buddha."
"If you violate this agreement, your punishment shall be unfathomable.

At that time, the King of Śrāvastī had a crown prince named Vairāṭa—so named because at the moment of his birth he was accompanied by a *vaidūrya* gem—which was leading a guard of soldiers to escort his maternal relatives when they were about to enter the city. Upon seeing the lecture hall, which was lofty, vast, solemn, pure, elegant, and exquisite—a rarity in the world—he halted there above it to rest in the cool shade.
The supervisor of the lecture hall went to inform the noble families, saying:
"The Prince of Śrāvastī has come and is staying in the lecture hall.
Upon hearing this, the noble families rose in anger and reviled him, saying:
"What extraordinary virtue does our household possess that we dare to enter this hall?

This temple was originally built for the sake of the Buddha; we ought to prepare the finest food and invite the World-Honored One, the Truly Enlightened One, along with his holy assembly. Only after the offerings are completed shall it be fitting for us to take up residence here."
Yet the lowly ones were placed before the honored, and their bodies were left here.

He immediately dispatched messengers to insult and humiliate them face-to-face, urging them to depart so they would not linger for long; he had the footprints they had trodden scraped away, and the jeweled steps they had stepped upon were promptly replaced with others.
At that time, Prince Vairāṭa heard the sound of that abuse; his countenance changed and his heart was filled with venomous anger. He commanded the chronicler, saying:
"Remember this well! When I become king, I shall execute those of such a kind."

The Grand Astrologer Asaṭha—translated into Chinese as Wuxin (Lack of Faith)—was capable of observing celestial phenomena and investigating portents and anomalies. He had this account written and placed inside his sash; harboring ill will and recognizing what was wrong, he sternly withdrew and returned home, never again going forward to pay court or visit his maternal relatives.
The Prince’s father, the King named Prasenajit, together with Queen Mallikā, traveled in a carriage with attendants to the Jeta Grove.

There, they alighted from the vehicle and set aside their parasols; they removed their crowns, unfastened their swords, put away their fly-whisks, took off their sandals, and dismissed the fourfold army.
Walking along a narrow path together with Mallikā, he prostrated himself on the ground with his five limbs touching it as a mark of reverence, then withdrew to sit to one side.
At that time, Prince Vairāṭa was returning to the palace;
seeing no one, he asked his attendants, "Where have the Father King and the Queen Mother gone?"
He replied, "To see the Buddha.
Upon hearing this question, the Prince was filled with joy; he led his followers without further disbanding their martial array and proceeded directly to the vihāra, saying:
"It is fitting that you know this is the time.

Thereupon, the Crown Prince slaughtered more than five hundred of the King's attendants and close ministers, exterminating them all at once. He removed the King’s crown, turban, parasol, sword, fly-whisk, shoes, robes, carriage, and all other ornaments, until there was not a single white object remaining outside.

At that time, the World-Honored One preached for the king and the queen verses on the impermanence of the world and the law of union and separation regarding desire; the king established himself in non-retrogression, and the queen attained the stage of the Path’s traces.

When the Buddha had finished preaching the sutra, the king bowed his head and withdrew; not seeing his attendants, he lay prostrate and disordered like a fallen corpse. Only the king’s robe and two attendants escaped, fleeing into the trees, where they later encountered the king again.
The king asked them,
"Where are the various officials?
The two men replied:
"The Crown Prince has led his subordinates and coerced them into returning to the palace.
The King said to Mallikā:
"Your son has committed an act of disobedience; he plots such rebellion as this."
"I have long known this; I shall now withdraw and entrust the kingdom to him at the vihāra.

To the left was a member of the nobility who, taking pity on the King and Queen—whose bodies were so delicate and their forms so frail that they could not endure walking—provided them with carriages. As these were dilapidated and difficult to manage, they eventually proceeded forward and reached the city gate.
Previously, the Crown Prince had stationed five hundred men at the gate as guards and commanded the gatekeeper, saying:
"If the Father King comes, do not allow him to enter."
The king said,
"If I am not permitted to enter, where shall I go?
He replied:
“Command the Great King to depart from the realm.
At that time, King Prasenajit wept and choked with sobs, and he praised him in verse:
“Truly indeed is the teaching of the World-Honored One; What has been expounded is examined and verified.”
Rise and fall, nobility and meanness—none of these possess permanence.
It is better to uphold the precepts and mind the Way than to covet generous stipends;
it is better to seek the opportunity to hear the Dharma assemblies than to desire hundreds of millions of lands.
"The King, ruling the state as he pleased, was greedy and depraved, indulging in whatever he desired;
yet, upon hearing the Dharma, he attained liberation, and his defilements were thereby eliminated.

At that time, there were countless thousands of onlookers who, hearing the King’s words of praise, eight hundred of them conceived the aspiration for the Great Way (bodhicitta) and all established themselves in the stage of non-retrogression, while their expressions turned from sorrowful to joyful.
Queen Mallikā said to the King, "Please do not be distressed;
let us go together and return to my father’s kingdom.
They set out immediately, and after seven days and seven nights, they arrived at the village of Tuṣa in Kapilavastu. It was already dark and the gates were closed, so they could not enter.

All were together afflicted by hunger and thirst, with no one to look up to for refuge and no place to beg; they stayed beside a stream where people were washing vegetables, and finding some stray radishes, they ate them and died from abdominal distension and pain.
The queen was overcome with grief and wailed aloud; those guarding the assembly asked, "Who is this?
She replied:
"I am the King's queen.
He asked again,
"Where is the King?"
The consort said:
"How tragic! The King has passed away by the water's edge."

The gatekeeper immediately galloped to inform the various noble Śākya clansmen. Upon hearing the tragic news, the nobles rushed there in shock and alarm; they soon all arrived, bringing funeral gifts and a coffin for the enshrinement, and performed the cremation according to the Dharma. They all wailed in grief, and none were moved by such profound sorrow.
At that time, the noble Śreṇika Bimbisāra—Gopī’s father—together with various prominent figures, praised him in verse:
"Having sons and wealth, one broods over them in restless agitation; Yet 'I' am not 'I,' so how can there be sons or wealth?
The foolish rely on themselves, yet even the powerful and honored have an end; The Prince, having used the kingdom, shall perish and enter hell."
Two hundred and fifty members of the noble Śākya clan, contemplating deeply the impermanence of existence, attained the stage of non-retrogression.
Five hundred women who had not yet left the household life attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Thereupon, when Prince Vairāṭya heard that his father, the King, had passed away, he immediately proclaimed himself sovereign from the palace and ascended the throne as king.
A court astrologer of a heterodox sect produced a secret state document, which served as evidence for the records of inauspicious omens and prohibitions based on past events.
Upon hearing this, he was filled with great rage; his mind was agitated and his spirit surged with indignation. He summoned the fourfold army and marched against Kapilavastu.
The Buddha, knowing his intent, emerged from the vihāra and took up position on the main road, sitting beneath a tree with withered roots.
In a brief moment, the Prince’s army arrived.

At that time, King Virūḍhaka saw the World-Honored One from afar and immediately descended from his elephant-chariot. He prostrated himself upon the ground and, kneeling for a long while, questioned the Buddha:
"O, Heaven among Heavens!..."

There are the bodhi, nyagrodha, pippala, udumbara, sāla, tala, and kaniṣkara trees; these seven trees have lofty and vast canopies and are lush with virtue. For what reason do you abandon them to dwell among withered, parched trees full of thorns?
The Buddha told King Virūḍhaka:
"Though there are seven trees with lush and flourishing shade, how could such abundance endure forever?
I sit beneath the thorn tree because I find it peaceful; it is for the sake of compassionately grieving for my kinsmen."
The king thought to himself:

"According to the secret prophecies recorded in the archives of antiquity, when an army on a military expedition encounters a śramaṇa, it must turn back its course; how much more so now that I have encountered the Buddha—how could I possibly advance?"
Having prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, they immediately turned their journey back.

Not long after returning to Śrāvastī, the attendant Ānanda and the Malla Lohitya escorted the World-Honored One back to the Nyagrodha Park; there, Ānanda was instructed to spread out seats and announce to the fourfold assembly that they were all to assemble.
At that time, the Buddha’s venerable countenance and features lacked their usual luster; his neck was without radiance, and his robes had changed color.
Having observed that the assembly was settled, Ānanda adjusted his dharma-robes, knelt with his right knee on the ground, pressed his palms together, and said:
"I have served the World-Honored One for many years, yet I have never before witnessed these three transformations."
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"In seven days from now, the noble clans of the Śākyas of Kapilavastu shall all suffer injury and death.
This manifestation of such a portent is because they have entered a period of mourning for a member of their own clan."
Mahāmaudgalyāyana came forward and addressed the World-Honored One:
"What need is there for such words?

As for my supernormal power, which the Perfectly Enlightened One has fully realized, I could take the kingdom of Śrāvastī with my right palm, leap it into the air, and hold it suspended—neither reaching the heavens above nor the earth below. How then could King Virūḍhaka have killed me?"
The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana:
"I am aware that your majestic power is already sufficient for this; as for the karmic offenses of your past lives, who else could take them upon themselves in your stead?
He spoke again:
“I can enclose this land with an iron lattice, shielding it from above with a bowl so that no signs of its form remain, and cast it away to another distant realm;
furthermore, I can split Mount Sumeru into four parts, place the southern portion within the mountain, and then rejoin them so that all find their own place of rest;

moreover, regarding the great ocean waters, deep and vast in measure at three million three hundred and thirty-six thousand *li*, I can place this land floating in its center, such that the people therein have no thought of coming or going.”
Furthermore, he can take this country and, relying upon the summit of Mount Sumeru, turn it upside down without causing any harm;

or he can submerge it down to the adamantine foundation of the earth; or he can hurl the fourfold armies of the Vaidūrya King onto the exterior of the Great Iron Ring Mountains, so that the two enemies do not engage in mutual warfare.
The Buddha said, "Excellent!
The World-Honored One trusts you; with these ten powers, you are able to accomplish this undertaking."
"Among the Śākyas, who among the nobility could endure the full retribution for their past misdeeds and sins, and take them upon themselves?
Ānanda said to the Buddha:
"Is there perhaps some miraculous being who protects this country, ensuring its peace and security?"
The Buddha said,
"If the people of Śrāvastī can remain united and do not maintain any ties of coming and going with external enemies, the kingdom may be preserved.
The Grand Astrologer remonstrated three times:
"The King ought to take this opportunity to advance and subdue the Śibis.
Upon hearing this, the king was filled with fierce anger; he raised his army and marshaled his troops.
The World-Honored One, knowing this, returned and sat beneath a withered tree.
Thus it happened three times, and the king likewise returned three times.
On the fourth expedition, as the Buddha would not yield, his elite fourfold army reached the borders of the Śākya kingdom.
The Śākya clan was of noble lineage, and many more had gathered there; they came forth to resist him. Their kinsmen were fierce and brave, powerful and skilled in archery:

some could shoot forty *li*, others twenty, ten, or seven. Each displayed his natural talent; their chariots could shatter flying objects at their first attempt, and their arrows never missed. They could split a single hair into seven strands, hitting their targets from a distance of several *li* with unerring precision; following the sound of the string, they struck their mark without fail.
Thereupon they engaged in battle, shooting at King Vairūḍaka’s army; they pierced banners and broke standards, tore off canopies and shattered their poles;
they cut through axles and yokes, and severed armor, belts, and breastplates;
they snapped the strings of bows and crossbows, yet did not harm the lives of elephants, horses, oxen, or other livestock.
He shot at his own ears, arms, fingers, rings, bracelets, and necklaces, yet they did not pierce his flesh;
he shaved off his beard, hair, eyebrows, whiskers, body hair, and eyelashes, yet these did not harm his body.
Vaiśravaṇa was terrified and asked his ministers,
"How far is the enemy from here,
that the arrows have reached this far and caused such destruction?"
He replied, "It is forty li, twenty li, or ten li; those nearest are seven li.
Upon hearing this, the king was seized with such trepidation that he could not find peace of mind; intending to destroy the enemy army, he immediately retreated in fear.
The Grand Historian remonstrated, saying:
"Your Majesty, do not fear!
Be most careful not to retreat."

The people of Śrāvastī all observe the precepts of the Buddha and serve as lay devotees; they are compassionate and benevolent, refraining from killing. Even when threatening others with arrows, they harbor no intent to harm; rather, they would sooner lose their own lives than take the life of another.
"Furthermore, let us reorganize our ranks and strike with one mind; by maintaining firm discipline and gravity, victory will not be long in coming.

The ministers replied, "Observing the enemy's archery, their arrows fall from afar without visible form; it is beyond our strength to resist them, and we fear being utterly crushed. We dread that you will forever cause us to be slaughtered, for we consider these arrows impossible to withstand. While we remain stationed here in safety, this minor official’s plan is not worth following exclusively. Each of us is moved by anxiety, our wills set on fleeing."
The king became greatly incensed and urgently commanded his troops to advance into battle.
The Śākyas and their external allies fled to take refuge within the city, closing the gates to fortify themselves and surrounding the enemy with drawn-up battle arrays.

Upon reaching the seventh day, he demonstrated his insight into what should be abandoned and what should be pursued; he sought to win them over and entice them in, proclaiming that the internal rebels should submit at once, for if they did not surrender, their kind would be utterly exterminated.

The Śākyas deliberated together: "Should we fortify the city for defense? Should we close the gates and prostrate ourselves? Or should we secretly flee in haste? As they hesitated in their distress, they each distributed counting-sticks to ascertain the consensus of the multitude.

Those who accepted the tally were many, while those who did not were few; by following the majority, they opened the gates to assist evil and bring about calamity. With internal and external forces responding to one another, they sought to ensure the enemy’s victory.

Those who exhorted him toward goodness were few; he gained entry through the gates, whereupon he slaughtered five hundred gatekeepers, inflicting incalculable harm and killing them. He bound thirty thousand persons of noble lineage alive and buried them in the ground, leaving only their heads exposed. He then drove herds of elephants over them until they were trampled to death by their feet, and subsequently yoked oxen to plows to furrow their heads. Among those who suffered such cruelty, there were all *srotāpannas*.
Śreṇika Bimbisāra’s old friend, Śreṇika Mānava, addressed his fellow countrymen, saying:

"Behold with clarity impermanence and its bitter, poisonous counterpart; past offenses must be repaid, so harbor no resentment. Life appears only to seek death; those who exist suddenly come to an end. Such manifold pains are like being split by axes at the five limbs."
He sighed deeply in lamentation:
"We shared the fortune of eating together, yet we must suffer calamity in one place.
Some seventy thousand members of the noble clans were born again and seen captured alive, their necks bound with iron chains.
He took a thousand women of noble lineage, strung them together with iron chains, and lined them up by the side of the road.
He placed the young children of noble families upon wooden frames and shot them to death.
At that time, King Virūḍhaka, seeing Śreṇika Bimbisāra’s son, Śākya-māna, together with the multitude in such hardship,
looked back and asked his minister, "Who is this man? The minister replied:
“Śreṇika, Śreṇika has come wishing to ask for something.
The king said:
"Show it. Śreṇika then declared:
"O Great King! [Show it to me.]"
"Your Majesty has treated me with great kindness and has graciously accepted what I have reported; I shall relate everything in detail.
The King understood the full circumstances and allowed him to speak freely.
"I pray that you will restrain your wrath and, for the time being, suspend the military operations so that they do not become reckless and cause further destruction."

"I shall enter the pond and return in a moment; we will deliberate in secret with the King so that a strategy may be seen immediately. Wait until I emerge from the water, and then you may once again deploy your troops.
The King thought to himself and said aloud:
"A man in the water cannot remain there for long."
He then granted the request.

Thereupon, Mānava, because the people of the kingdom had encountered a great calamity, took his leave and entered the pond; he untied his hair, tied it to a tree, and submerged himself in the water, yet after a long while he did not return.

The King was greatly astonished by this and immediately dispatched his attendants to search for him; beneath the roots of the tree, they found his corpse, which they brought out and interred beside the pond.
The king felt great pity for him and was moved by a heart of compassion:
"For the sake of his family and clan, he has drowned himself; such is the nature of his righteousness.
As the sovereign of this land, I cannot bear to harbor a petty resentment. Why should I engage in a swift battle that would cause further harm to escalate?"
The first three hundred million people faced their end together and perished;
the next three hundred million were spared by the grace of the subsequent [intervention], being rescued so that they all regained their breath, fleeing and escaping to preserve their lives.

Furthermore, another three hundred million people maintained domestic offerings, feasting with joy and merriment, amusing themselves with music and dance; unaware of the external calamity of collective death and hearing nothing of the terror of flight, they remained as peaceful and composed as usual, unconcerned with anything beyond themselves.

King Vīḍūḍabha gave Maṇibhadda a grand funeral and continued to favor his descendants. After King Vīḍūḍabha had pacified the Śākyas and established a new leader, he completed his consolations and returned to the kingdom of Śrāvastī.

The Buddha and his disciples arrived at Kapilavastu and saw that many among the people were maimed and injured. He further observed many women who were deprived of their hands, feet, ears, noses, and limbs; their bodies were exposed and they lay abandoned in ditches and trenches, with nothing to cover themselves. Such was the suffering of the world, where uncompassionate men inflict such extreme cruelty upon one another.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:

"That King Vīrūḍhaka acted with such unrestrained malice and rebellion that his transgressions have now reached such a height. In seven days, the fires of hell shall come to burn and kill him; having committed a crime in this present life, he shall receive its retribution in this very life."

The Grand Astrologer presented the prophecy, which was found to be identical to that concerning the Buddha; the King was seized with great terror and boarded a ship to enter the sea, hoping to escape his fate, remaining there upon the high seas.
When the seven-day period came to an end, a natural fire spontaneously emerged from the water, incinerating the ship and the king, reducing them all at once to ashes.

Out of compassion for those who were naked and suffering, the World-Honored One used his majestic spiritual power to move the purple-gem palace of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. Śakra, his queen, Suyāma, and countless other sons of heaven each brought celestial robes and descended together to offer them, clothing and covering all those who were naked and in distress.
The Buddha spoke these verses for the sake of the women:
"What you all see with your eyes, Is the transformation occurring in the present.
Having exhausted the old, do not create the new; Thus, in the future, you may attain lasting liberation."
After the Buddha had finished reciting these verses, he further preached the Dharma for them.

Among the countless thousands of onlookers—gods, nāgas, spirits, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, brahmins, householders, elders, and common people—who heard what the Buddha taught, five hundred bhikṣus attained the exhaustion of outflows and liberation of mind;
five hundred brahmins and other present individuals, having witnessed the pain of their country’s ruin and devastation, left the household life to follow the Way and all became śramaṇas.
Five hundred devaputras attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas;
two hundred asuras and a thousand nāga kings all resolved to attain unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment;
and the five stumps in the ditches and the naked men and women, at the end of their lives, were reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
Fifteen hundred people attained the path of vision,
and one thousand attained the realization of non-returning.
When the Buddha had finished speaking these words, everyone heard them throughout, prostrated themselves, and withdrew.
The Sūtra on King Virūḍhaka Spoken by the Buddha
